text:
Cross border banking is still far from seamless, especially for freelancers, remote workers, and digital nomads. @tryavvio  is building a simpler solution by combining global banking, crypto, and DeFi into one app.

With Avvio users can access virtual USD and EUR accounts, spend worldwide using a Visa card, manage crypto through a self custodial wallet, and earn yield via DeFi all from a single platform.

What sets it apart is its focus on user ownership. Private keys remain under the user's control through Turnkey, while financial data is encrypted using @SeismicSys's privacy first infrastructure.

As of July 2026, the app is already live on iOS and Android, backed by partnerships with Turnkey, MoonPay, Bridge, Blend, Relay, and Seismic. No token has been launched yet, making Avvio a project worth watching as it continues to grow.

author: marlowxbt
text:
The most underrated desk upgrade of the year is free. It uses the iPad you already own.

A guy on GitHub released OpenSidecar. Free. Open source. peetzweg/opensidecar. You install it on a Mac and any spare Apple device becomes a full second monitor. An old iPad. An iPhone. A second MacBook.

Not a mirror. A real extension of your desktop. You drag a browser window from the Mac straight onto the iPad, scroll with your finger, move around the page like the tablet is a monitor you can hold.

Until this week, that feature cost $100. Duet Display. Luna Display. Apple's own Sidecar with a locked list of supported devices. Three paid products doing what one open source repo now does over Wi-Fi or USB with macOS 14 and iOS 17.

The real idea in the post is not the app.

The real idea is that half the people watching have an iPad in a drawer that became a YouTube player, then a coaster, then dust. It has an M1 chip and a retina display and it is sitting three feet from a laptop that would kill for the extra screen.

Do not buy a second monitor. You already have one. You forgot about it.

The demo is a live prototype. Latency under video editing and games has not been tested. But for a browser window, a Notion doc, a Slack, a spreadsheet, it just works.

The best desk upgrade of the year is not a new display. It is the device you already stopped using.

author: tekscreate
text:
Google AI Studio just landed on iPhone — and the App Store listing reveals something interesting.

114 MB binary. iOS 18+. 76 languages. Released July 1, 2026.

This isn't just a mobile port of the web interface. At 114 MB for a cloud-first product, they're bundling meaningful local modules — likely on-device prompt processing, offline caching, and local inference for small models.

The bigger story: Google is making a direct play for the "vibe coding" workflow on mobile. The tagline is "build your ideas wherever inspiration strikes" — which translates to: you can prototype, test prompts, and iterate on AI apps from your phone without touching a laptop.

Competitive positioning matters here:
- OpenAI has the ChatGPT app (chat-first, not build-first)
- Anthropic has Claude on mobile (conversation, not prototyping)
- Google AI Studio Mobile is build-first — it's Gemini's API playground in your pocket

For developers who prototype on the go — this changes the mobile workflow significantly. Pre-order is live, full launch is here.

https://t.co/8eB04DowFW

author: tekscreate
text:
Meta quietly launched Pocket — an AI app that generates playable mini-games and interactive apps from a text prompt.

The company calls these "gizmos." Describe what you want, and Pocket builds a playable interactive experience — complete with touch reactions, camera access, sound effects, and phone-movement sensing. You can publish to a discovery feed where others play or remix your gizmo.

Key details:
- Launched June 29 on iOS and Android
- Built from Gizmo technology — Meta hired the Gizmo team earlier this year and licensed their tech
- Gizmo had 635K installs with 98% positive sentiment
- Meta's Superintelligence Labs is behind it
- Still in early testing — not available everywhere yet

This is a different bet than Meta's other AI products. Meta AI generates images. Vibes generates videos. Pocket generates *interactivity* — apps and games that react to touch, movement, and the real world through your camera.

The Gizmo acquisition makes more sense now. Meta didn't just buy a team — they bought a distribution model for AI-generated software. Think of it as the TikTok of mini-apps, but instead of scrolling videos, you're scrolling playable AI-generated experiences.

The question: will the quality bar hold up when millions of users start generating gizmos? Gizmo's 98% positive sentiment on 635K installs suggests a tight feedback loop. Scaling that without quality degradation is the hard part.

Download link is live on both stores if you want to try it.

author: tekscreate
text:
Google just shipped a dictation app that runs entirely offline, strips filler words in real time, and it's free.

AI Edge Eloquent is on iOS now. Speak, pause, and it cleans up every "um" and "uh" automatically. If you want more, connect Gmail to import your jargon and toggle Gemini online features for smart rewrites.

Why this matters: it runs on-device via Google's Gemma architecture. No data leaves your phone unless you opt into the Gemini layer. That's a privacy-first approach to a category that's been dominated by cloud-dependent tools.

The polish features are genuinely useful:
- Raw speech → clean readable text
- Key points extraction (online mode)
- Formal/short/long rewrites
- Speaking speed stats (WPM tracking)

The big question: when does this hit Android? Google launching an iOS-first AI app is unusual — suggests they're testing the product-market fit before the full rollout.

For devs who dictate PRDs, code comments, or docs on the go — this is worth a download.

https://t.co/YSY0y4yXqz
